adjudicated.claim: min_sigma[err(g)+Pr[f!=g]+L ln2/m] <= err(f)+eps+(ln2/m)K_eps(f). The parenthetical says the rough form 'ignores the variance factor in the binomial inversion, which only helps at small errors'. The intro says the Occam bound gives err(g) <= training error + about L ln2/m.
adjudicated.why_wrong: Take the sigma that attains K_eps. Then err(g) <= err(f)+Pr[f!=g] <= err(f)+eps, and Pr[f!=g] <= eps again, so the right side is err(f)+2*eps+..., not +eps. The parenthetical also has the direction backwards. At nonzero training error q the binomial inversion is about q+sqrt(2qL ln2/m)+L ln2/m. Dropping the square-root term makes the rough form optimistic, not conservative. 'Training error plus L ln2/m' is the realizable rate only.
adjudicated.failure_scenario: Labels are deterministic and f is correct everywhere (err(f)=0). The only short g has Pr[f!=g]=eps, so err(g)=eps. The reduction then gives 2*eps+K_eps ln2/m, which exceeds the displayed right side. Measured case: maj5 with 10% label noise at m=16000 has bound minus test error = 0.174-0.139 = 0.035, while L ln2/m = 53*0.693/16000 = 0.0023. The gap is the sqrt term, which the paper calls helpful.
adjudicated.suggested_fix: Write err(f)+2*eps+... (or err(f)+eps+... with eps defined through err(g)-err(f)). State that the fast L ln2/m rate holds only when err(g) is near 0 and that otherwise the deviation is about sqrt(err(g) L ln2/m). Fix the parenthetical.

verdict.explanation:
I checked this against the current files on branch claude/friendly-wright-x6ajj5. The defect is real, but it is minor.

(1) Factor 2. paper/sections/discussion.tex:5 states a hard inequality, min_sigma[err(g)+Pr[f!=g]+L ln2/m] <= err(f)+eps+(ln2/m)K_eps(f). The only justification available is to plug in the sigma* that attains K_eps. That gives err(g*) <= err(f)+Pr[f!=g*] <= err(f)+eps, so the bracket is at most err(f)+2eps+K_eps ln2/m. The reviewer's counterexample is valid. Take deterministic labels and err(f)=0. Let the shortest g with Pr[f!=g]<=eps have Pr[f!=g]=eps and err(g)=eps, and let every description with smaller disagreement be longer than K_eps+eps*m/ln2. Then the minimum is min(2eps+K_eps ln2/m, ...), which is greater than eps+K_eps ln2/m. The '<=' is false as written. In the label-noise case the factor does not bite, because g is the clean rule and err(g)<err(f), but the display claims it in general.

(2) The parenthetical, 'this rough form ignores the variance factor in the binomial inversion, which only helps at small errors', is backwards or at least inconsistent. The term L ln2/m is the inversion at zero training error, the fast rate that the variance-sensitive (kl) form gives. At training error q the inversion is about q+sqrt(2qc)+c with c=(L ln2+ln 1/delta)/m. So the rough form understates the true bound whenever err(g) is not small; it is not conservative. If 'ignoring the variance factor' means replacing p(1-p) by 1/4, that gives the Hoeffding rate sqrt(L ln2/2m), not the L ln2/m in the display. Either way the parenthetical misdescribes the display. I checked the numbers (scipy, 1 thread) for the case the paragraph cites, maj5 with 10% label noise at m=16000, L=49+4=53 bits, delta1=0.025. Bin(1600,16000,delta1 2^-53)-0.1=0.0218, while L ln2/m=0.0023, so the ignored term is about 9 times the displayed one. The summary row in results/boolean/summary_n50.md agrees: Occam part 0.1232 against err(g)=0.1, bound 0.1741 against test error 0.1390. The 0.035 gap is about 0.022 from the sqrt term plus about 0.01 of triangle slack (0.2*Pr[f!=g]). So the reviewer's 'the gap is the sqrt term' is right for about two thirds of it.

(3) intro.tex:9 and README.md:9 say the Occam bound gives 'training error plus about L ln2/m'. That is right only when the training error of g is near zero, and the paper's own noisy-label surrogates have training error about 0.1. A related unflagged instance is experiments.tex:9: 'Across the learning curve the bound is roughly test error plus L ln2/m' fails for the noisy-label rows (gap 0.035 against 0.0023) and for junta6 at m=2000 (gap 0.17 against about 0.035).

What I checked and found correct: Theorem 2 (theory.tex:16-24) and Lemma 1's kl relaxation are stated correctly, and every computed bound uses the exact binomial inversion, so no reported number is affected. verdict.explanation:
I checked the current files: paper/sections/abstract.tex, intro.tex:16, experiments.tex:9, README.md:26, paper/tables/boolean_n50.tex, results/boolean/summary_n50.md, the per-seed rows in results/boolean/grid_n50.jsonl, and code/cgb/boolean.py (compress, truth_table_from_pool, final_bound). The round-1 record in verification/README.md does not cover this item.

What is wrong. experiments.tex:9 says "Across the learning curve the bound is roughly test error plus L ln2/m". It also says the bound "still tracks" where f has only partly learned the target, citing only parity3 at m=2000 (0.29 against 0.30). The abstract, intro and README say the bound "tracks the test error of f along the whole learning curve". The paper's own table contradicts this for partly trained junta6 networks:
- m=1000: test error 0.311, bound 0.645. Test error plus L ln2/m (78 bits) predicts about 0.365.
- m=2000: test error 0.1685, bound 0.342. The formula (102 bits) predicts about 0.20.

The per-seed rows show why. The chosen g ("table k=6") makes 157 to 229 training errors out of 2000, so its Occam term is 0.17 to 0.21, not the 0.036 that zero training errors would give. The cause is in the code: truth_table_from_pool fills each cell of the table with the majority of f's own predictions on a pool. In cells where f is mostly wrong, g differs from the target, and f is right on the training points in those cells. Pointwise, err(g) + Pr[f!=g] = err(f) + 2 Pr[f right, g wrong], so the reduction can cost up to about twice err(f), plus the Occam and square-root slack. Other partly trained rows behave the same way, with the bound well above the test error:
- fullmaj m=500: test error 0.066, bound 0.26; g makes 11 to 13 training errors.
- maj5 with noise, m=500 to 2000: test error about 0.20, bounds 0.30 to 0.40.

So the "test + L ln2/m" sentence is wrong for those rows, and "tracks along the whole learning curve" overstates how tight the bound is. The parity3 m=2000 case is tight only because the cell majority of f there happens to equal the true parity, so g makes zero training errors.

What is not a defect. "parity3 at m<=1000 is vacuous, correctly" is right. Test error there is 0.496, so any valid bound must be at least about 0.5. Vacuity is the correct outcome, whether the bound is 0.97 or 1.0. The noisy rows at m=16000 (0.17 against 0.14) and "within 0.005 at m=16000" for the clean tasks match the table. All bounds are at or above their test errors, and the table entries match the summary file.

adjudicated.claim: 'From a typical initialization, wide networks trained by gradient descent approach a deterministic limit (the kernel or the mean-field limit), so the initialization only adds fluctuations of order width^{-1/2}.'
adjudicated.why_wrong: In the NTK/kernel limit the tangent kernel becomes deterministic, but the network at initialization converges to a nondegenerate Gaussian process. The trained function f_0 + K(.,X)K^{-1}(y - f_0(X)) depends on the random initialization at order 1, not width^{-1/2}. Only mean-field (1/width) scaling gives a deterministic limit with vanishing initial function. The paper's own lazy regime (init scale 2) is the NTK case. theory/README.md item (iv) says the opposite ('theta_0-dependent noise plus a dense small update').
adjudicated.failure_scenario: Two lazily trained 512-unit networks from different seeds differ at order 1 on inputs away from the training set. A weight-space codec must pay for that order-1 initial function, not width^{-1/2} fluctuations, which affects the answer to research question 3.
adjudicated.suggested_fix: Restrict the claim to mean-field scaling, or to an antisymmetrized/centred initialization with f_0 = 0. For the kernel regime, state that the initial function is an O(1) Gaussian-process sample that the trained function inherits.

verdict.severity: wrong-claim, minor in impact: it sits in the discussion and the README summary and affects no bound, table or number, but as written it misstates a standard result and gives the wrong answer to the user's question about initialization.
verdict.explanation:
I checked the current files: the working tree for these files matches HEAD bdb413ee, and only results/ files have changed. The sentence is still there word for word in paper/sections/discussion.tex:11, item (iv): "wide networks trained by gradient descent approach a deterministic limit (the kernel or the mean-field limit), so the initialization only adds fluctuations of order width^{-1/2}". README.md:43 makes the same claim without the order: "Wide networks approach a deterministic limit, and the initialization contributes only fluctuations." verification/README.md does not list it as fixed.

The claim is right for mean-field scaling and wrong for the kernel (NTK/lazy) limit.
- **Mean-field:** the dynamics converge to a deterministic limit, and fluctuations are O(width^{-1/2}).
- **Kernel limit:** only the tangent kernel becomes deterministic (Jacot et al. 2018). The initial function f_{theta_0} converges to a Gaussian-process sample of order one. The trained function f_inf(x) = f_0(x) + Theta(x,X)Theta(X,X)^{-1}(y - f_0(X)) is therefore random at order one. Lee et al. 2019 give its nonzero, width-independent variance.

**Numerical check** (/tmp/claude-0/referee2/ntk_var.py, one thread, closed-form infinite-width kernels): for a one-hidden-layer ReLU network in NTK parametrization, d=30, m=300 random points of {+-1}^30, and 500 test points, the variance of the trained function over initializations is 0.058 on average (min 0.030), against a prior variance K(x,x)=0.5. That is a standard deviation of about 0.24 on +-1 targets, and it does not shrink with width.

**The paper's own setup is the kernel case.** Its "lazy" regime (code/experiments/init_kernel.py:50-51, init_scale=2.0 with SGD) is exactly this case, with a nonzero f_0, which the code computes explicitly at lines 107-108. theory/README.md (iv) already says so ("in the lazy regime the trained function is theta_0-dependent noise plus a dense small update"). The discussion and README contradict both.

**Correction to the reviewer's failure scenario:** a weight-space codec does not pay for the order-one f_0 itself, because theta_0 comes from a data-independent seed and is free (Lemma 8 / lem:init). What depends on theta_0 at order one is the trained function. The update also has to cancel f_0 on the training points. So the follow-on sentence "a weight-space codec must pay for them or certify through them" should be reworded along with (iv).

verdict.severity: minor (wrong-claim about prior work; it overstates novelty in a remark and in theory/README, and no result depends on it)
verdict.explanation:
The defect is real for the Nagarajan & Kolter (2019) half of the sentence. I checked the current files at HEAD bdb413ee. The arXiv abstract would not load from here (DNS failure and proxy 403), so the description of N&K below comes from my recollection of their ICLR 2019 abstract and method, cross-checked against the project's own files.

The current text:
- `paper/sections/theory.tex:99` (Remark, relation to PAC-Bayes) says: "The margin-based derandomizations of \citet{neyshabur2018pacbayes} and \citet{nagarajan2019deterministic} instead control the perturbation's effect uniformly over inputs, with norm-based bounds."
- `theory/README.md:99` says Theorem 5 works "through a per-input concentration statement instead of a sup over all inputs (as in the margin-based derandomizations of Neyshabur et al. 2018 and Nagarajan & Kolter 2019)."

Neyshabur et al. (2018):
- Here the sentence is correct.
- Their derandomization lemma needs, with probability at least 1/2 over the perturbation u, max_{x in X} |f_{w+u}(x) - f_w(x)|_inf < gamma/4. That is a sup over all inputs of bounded norm, controlled through products of spectral norms.

Nagarajan & Kolter (2019):
- The sentence is wrong. Their stated key novelty is that conditions on the weight matrices, checked on the training data and implying a wide training-loss minimum, themselves generalize to test data. The conditions are input-dependent: pre-activation magnitudes, hidden-layer norms and Jacobian norms at each input.
- Their perturbation analysis is per input. With Gaussian weight noise at a fixed input, the layer error is about sigma*||h(x)||*sqrt(log), an l2 typical-case quantity, not a sup over inputs. They advertise that the result avoids the product of spectral norms that the uniform route needs.
- So the structure the remark presents as the contrast — a per-input, typical-case condition on training points transferred to test points — is the defining feature of N&K 2019.

The project contradicts itself here:
- `paper/sections/related.tex:9` says these derandomizations use robustness "checked on the training data". It also says the dithered theorem "shares their structure (a perturbation set around f plus a per-point condition transferred from training to test)".
- `literature.md:243` lists N&K as "Noise-resilience on training points, proved to generalize to test points".

The remark therefore credits Theorem 5 with a difference that does not separate it from N&K. The real differences are:
- a single public dither draw with an Occam code of g, instead of a Gaussian posterior and its KL;
- a certificate computed from the coded g;
- non-vacuous values on narrow and sparse-update MNIST networks.

Related errors:
- `literature.md:416` says the same thing ("or are worst-case and vacuous (Neyshabur 2018; Nagarajan–Kolter 2019)").
- `related.tex:9` ("per-input concentration bound in place of worst-case or norm-based perturbation bounds") is defensible, because N&K's per-input bounds are still norm-based, and it already concedes the shared per-point transfer structure.

Nothing else needs to change. The abstract's "removes the sqrt(d) loss of worst-case perturbation sets" compares with the paper's own Theorem 4. The intro and top-level README only say N&K is vacuous, which is not disputed.

The reviewer's suggestion to cite Langford & Shawe-Taylor (2002) is optional and not needed for correctness; that work is not in refs.bib.

with:

The trained f would also be a different network. Such a D puts no constraint on the bound at this S, so the sentence "That is correct: an input distribution concentrated on the exceptions would make f wrong almost always" mixes up a fixed f with the S-dependent f_S.
